subject: research/mimic-batch
professional: a statistician who has refereed work on classifier evaluation and text-provenance detection (a trust-and-safety ML scientist or a sequential-testing statistician). They would check first whether the false-positive rate of a batch verdict is estimated with the uncertainty it deserves (one calibration/test split per family is a single draw), whether the mean is the right pooling statistic against the Wald likelihood-ratio benchmark, and whether the i.i.d.-with-replacement batch model is a fair stand-in for one account's texts

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 batch.py` (about 90 s, scipy and scikit-learn installed via pyenv.py): results.txt byte-identical to the committed copy and `git status` clean for results.json, so the artefact is current and deterministic (seed 0). Recomputed outside batch.py: (1) the README's mean rows from results.json (my own numpy means over the 8 families) match every table cell to 3 decimals, e.g. k=1 AUROC 0.935 and FPR 0.074, k=32 FPR 0.150, k=8 p=0.1 AUROC 0.732; (2) batch.auroc against a brute-force O(n*m) pairwise count on random normals: 0.7915333 both; (3) per-text (k=1) AUROC from my own pairwise comparison of the held-out family scores (own fit through threshold.fit, test on all 300 vs 300 texts): recipes 0.867 (results 0.877), books 0.993 (0.992), wiki 0.895 (0.90), agreeing within sampling of the half-split; (4) the k=32 FPR with my own parity split (own code, 20000 batches): recipes 0.144, books 0.016, wiki 0.001, against the published 0.011, 0.596, 0.124. The arithmetic is right, but the headline FPR numbers are one random split: 12 seeds per family (nb=1000) give a k=32 FPR range of 0.00 to 0.61 per family and a family-averaged mean of 0.100, not the 0.150 reported; the k=1 mean over splits is about 0.055, not 0.074. Direction of the effect (FPR inflates with k) holds in every family's mean; its size and which family is worst do not. Not scored 4 since the reported magnitudes are not stable.
evidence.completeness: Every README claim was checked and worked end to end: tests (7 listed, 7 found and pass), batch.py writes results.json and results.txt, figure.py and experiments/figure.svg exist, the table, the per-family rows (results.txt has 48 rows: 8 families x 6 k), the skipped-cell rule (round(p*k)=0) and the live-page and link lines. No stubs or TODOs. The 'Next steps' (SPRT, max statistic, correlated batches, adapted imitators) are honestly labelled as not done, so the stated scope is complete; the scope itself is a single statistic and a single detector.
evidence.verification: `python3 -m pytest tests -q`: 7 passed in 0.74 s. Two hand-seeded mutations in batch.py, each reverted with git checkout (status clean afterwards). (1) simulate(): threshold taken at quantile `target` instead of `1 - target`: caught by test_fpr_near_target_and_tpr_grows_with_k. (2) simulate(): test half set equal to the calibration half (`sh[idx[:n//2]]` twice, i.e. the calibration/test split leaks, which is exactly the effect the README's headline finding is about): all 7 tests passed, so it survived. No test uses the split at all: none checks that the FPR on the test half can differ from the calibration half, none runs main() or touches the real data, and the FPR test uses i.i.d. normals where calibration and test halves are exchangeable by construction, so cannot reveal the headline phenomenon. The helpers (auroc, batch_means, mixed_means) are well tested.
evidence.craft: Read batch.py (88 lines), tests/test_batch.py, and the imported threshold.py loader and fit. Compact, vectorised, readable, seeded, with docstrings and edge-case handling (m == 0, k - m == 0). Defects: tests never touch main(); `import scipy` inside auroc() is a lazy import for no reason; the module inserts into sys.path to import a sibling project (fragile; fine for this repo layout); results written without a context manager (open(...) not closed); single seed, no repeat loop or CI machinery even though it is one line away; the per-text threshold reuses the same rng stream so cells are not independent of each other (benign). No silent fallback found.
evidence.claims: Checked against files: every table number (results.json/txt, verified above); '7 tests' (true); 'about 2 minutes' (true); '4,000 batches per cell' (NB=4000, true); 'books 60%, poetry 26%, wiki 12%' (results.txt: 0.596, 0.261, 0.124, true as a single draw); 'extends mimic-recalib ... needs about 80 calibration texts' (not re-checked against that project). Unbacked or overstated: the prose presents 'the human batches flagged are ... 15% on average at k = 32 and 60% for books' and 'the bigger the batch, the more calibration texts the human baseline needs' as a finding, but the one-split design cannot separate a systematic bias from split luck, and my 12-seed rerun shows the family numbers swing from about 0 to 0.6 and the mean is 0.10. The Limitations section does say 'one split per family, no confidence intervals', which is honest, but the Results bullets and the title question ('how many texts does a detector need') state the numbers without that qualifier. The dilution rule 'about a factor of the machine share' is a rough reading of 4 rows, no fit. Preliminary label, assistant disclosure, no-lab-affiliation line and the i.i.d. caveat are present. No disclaimer needed for research.
evidence.fitness: The job: a researcher or moderator asks how many texts from one source a weak detector needs. The researcher can reuse batch.py and the pooling result. The finding that AUROC saturates fast under independence is nearly a restatement of the central limit theorem plus the per-text AUROC, and the result that matters operationally (a calibrated verdict) is the unstable one. Nearest prior work: Wald 1945 and the SPRT (cited but not implemented, the obvious optimal comparator), Chakraborty et al. 2023 'On the possibilities of AI-generated text detection' (sample-complexity of detection grows with the number of samples), Sadasivan et al. 2025 (cited), and the Neyman-Pearson / multiple-sample detection literature; the repository's own mimic-recalib already shows calibration-set size matters for single texts. So the novelty is the batch extension on real RAID data, which is modest and only partly sound: the sound part is the direction (a finite calibration set hurts more as k grows, which is expected from the 1/sqrt(k) shrinkage the README explains correctly), the unsound part is the quantified FPR. i.i.d. resampling from 300 texts and no correlated-author batches make the deployment reading optimistic. Not publishable without CIs over splits, the SPRT or max comparator, and correlated batches.
evidence.domain: Compared with standard practice in detection-theory and classifier evaluation: (a) pooling by mean score is a defensible baseline but a statistician expects the LLR sum/SPRT or a Fisher/Stouffer combination; for the 10%-machine case the README itself says max or count would suit better and did not test it; (b) threshold calibration by a held-out human quantile is standard, but reporting the realised FPR from one split without an interval or a repeated-split (cross-validation) estimate is below the standard for a false-accusation claim; (c) batching by bootstrap with replacement from the same 150 texts that supplied the null underestimates variance at k=32 (duplicates, 150-text pool), which is probably part of the inflated FPR; (d) the detector's AUROC of 0.935 averages out family heterogeneity (recipes 0.88) correctly noted. Departures are named in the README's Limitations, which keeps this at 2 rather than 1.

defects.what: The headline false-positive finding (mean k=32 FPR 15%, books 60%, poetry 26%) is a single random calibration/test split per family. Rerunning with 12 other seeds gives a per-family k=32 range of 0.00 to 0.61 and a family-averaged FPR of about 0.10; k=1 FPR averages about 0.055 over splits, not 0.074. With a parity split books drops to 1.6% and recipes rises to 14%. A reader acting on 'books 60%' would misjudge a detector's reliability; the direction is real, the magnitudes and the worst-family identity are split luck.
defects.where: research/mimic-batch/batch.py:46-63, research/mimic-batch/README.md (Results, third and fourth bullets)

defects.what: Mutation making the test half identical to the calibration half (removing the very split the headline finding depends on) passes all 7 tests; no test checks a calibration/test difference, and the FPR test uses exchangeable i.i.d. normals.

Batches are bootstrap draws with replacement from a 150-text calibration pool and 150-text test pool; at k=32 duplicates are frequent and the null variance of the batch mean is underestimated relative to genuinely distinct texts, an unquantified contributor to the FPR inflation. The nearest sound comparator (SPRT, which the README cites) is not implemented.
main() is untested and writes result files without closing handles; scipy imported lazily inside auroc().

verdict: The code runs, the tests pass, results.txt reproduces byte-for-byte, and every number in the README table matches results.json and my own recomputation, with per-text AUROC and the batch AUROC arithmetic confirmed independently. But the part of the story with consequences, the false-accusation rate that grows with batch size, rests on one random split per family; rerunning with other seeds shows the family values spanning 0 to 0.6 and the average at 0.10 instead of 0.15, so the quantified claim is not stable even though the direction is. The tests would not catch a calibration/test leak (a seeded mutation survived), and the study omits the standard comparator (SPRT) and any author-correlated batches. This is honest preliminary work with its limits written down (claims 2 not lower for that reason), at roughly junior-to-mid statistical level: correctness 3 (arithmetic and reproduction), but verification 2 and claims 2 mean it does not meet the bar. Scores are before any fix.
